questions.question: What does the Compose compiler plugin add to every composable function's signature?
options: A Context parameter and a LifecycleOwner parameter for the host
A unique String ID used to look up its slot
A CoroutineScope parameter so the function can suspend
A Composer parameter plus an Int bitmask of change info
questions.explanation: The plugin appends `$composer` and `$changed` (and `$default` when there are default arguments). The Composer carries the composition, and `$changed` lets callers pass what they know about whether arguments changed. Composables are not suspend functions.

questions.question: Since Kotlin 2.0 the Compose compiler lives in the Kotlin repository and ships with the same version number as Kotlin, applied via the org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose Gradle plugin.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: From Kotlin 2.0 the Compose compiler moved into the Kotlin project, so there is no separate compiler version to match against Kotlin any more. You apply the Compose Compiler Gradle plugin and configure it in the composeCompiler block.

questions.question: What information does the `$changed` bitmask carry into a composable?
options: A few bits per parameter: static, same, changed or uncertain
A count of how many times the function has been recomposed
A flag telling the function which thread it is running on
A hash of all the arguments, computed by the caller before the call
questions.explanation: Each parameter gets a small group of bits: uncertain, same, different or static. If the caller already knows an argument is unchanged or static, the callee can skip its own equality check. Otherwise the callee compares with the stored value from the slot table.

questions.question: Why does the compiler pass a `$default` bitmask instead of relying on Kotlin's normal default-argument mechanism?
options: Kotlin default arguments don't work on functions with more than 22 parameters
So default expressions, which may be composable, run inside the function
So default values are saved in the Bundle across process death
So defaults can be changed at runtime by the Recomposer
questions.explanation: Defaults like `color: Color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primary` call composables, so they must be evaluated inside the function with the composer available and in the right group. The bitmask says which arguments were omitted so the function computes those defaults itself.

questions.question: Which statements about the groups the compiler generates are true? Select all that apply.
options: Every composable call is wrapped in a movable group by default
A restartable composable registers a lambda at the end of its group to re-run it when invalidated
Inline composables such as Column don't get a restart group of their own
Composables that return a value are not restartable
questions.explanation: Restartable Unit-returning composables end with a restart scope whose update lambda calls the function again. Inline functions and value-returning composables can't be restarted alone, so their reads invalidate the caller. Movable groups are for key() and similar identity-based cases, not the default.

questions.question: With strong skipping (default since Kotlin 2.0.20), how is the non-composable lambda passed to onClick handled when it captures an unstable object?
options: It is recreated every recomposition, making Button impossible to skip
It is hoisted into a static singleton, since all lambdas are stateless
It is remembered, keyed on its captures, unstable ones compared by ===
The compiler reports an error asking you to wrap it in remember yourself
questions.explanation: Under strong skipping the compiler wraps lambdas in a remember keyed by their captured values, comparing stable captures with equals and unstable ones with ===. As long as the same viewModel and id are captured, the same lambda instance is reused and Button can skip. Before strong skipping, lambdas with unstable captures were not memoized.

questions.question: The compiler wraps composable lambdas (such as a `content: @Composable () -> Unit` argument) in a remembered runtime object, so the same instance is reused and the lambda body can recompose on its own.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Composable lambdas are wrapped in a runtime object that is remembered (or made a singleton when it captures nothing) and has its own restart scope. The parent can then skip while only the lambda body re-runs when state it reads changes.

questions.question: What is the effect of annotating a small composable with @NonRestartableComposable?
options: It can never be called from a restartable composable
It always recomposes on every frame, even when none of its inputs changed
Its remembered values are discarded at every recomposition
It gets no restart group, so its reads invalidate the caller's scope
questions.explanation: Without a restart group the function can't be re-run by itself, so invalidations go to the nearest restartable ancestor. This removes some overhead for tiny functions that just forward to another composable. It doesn't affect remember or force per-frame recomposition.

questions.question: Which of these does the Compose compiler plugin do? Select all that apply.
options: Wraps if/when branches in groups so positional identity stays stable
Turns composable functions into suspend functions under the hood
Inserts start/end group calls keyed by integers derived from source location
Infers the stability of classes in modules it compiles
Creates a ViewModel scope for each composable function
questions.explanation: The plugin inserts groups with source-based keys (including around control flow), adds the synthetic parameters, and infers stability for skipping. Composables are not coroutines: they're called synchronously with a Composer. ViewModel scoping comes from ViewModelStoreOwners, not the compiler.

questions.question: What does skipping look like in the code the compiler generates for a skippable composable?
options: The function runs fully, but the Applier ignores its node changes
If inputs are unchanged and skipping is allowed, it skips to its group end
The caller removes the call from the bytecode once it has run once
The function returns a cached View object from the previous composition
questions.explanation: At the top of the body, generated code checks `$changed` and stored values; if nothing changed and the composer allows skipping, it calls skipToGroupEnd so the previous slots and nodes are reused. Running the body and then discarding changes would waste the work skipping is meant to save.
